cv-bbed1d1f.stem: Where do the hepatic veins open?
options: Directly into the inferior vena cava
cv-bbed1d1f.explanation: The three large hepatic veins open directly into the IVC on the posterior surface of the liver. The portal vein, by contrast, brings blood to the liver.

cv-2673b4e2.stem: Which structures drain cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) into the superior sagittal sinus?
cv-2673b4e2.explanation: CSF is produced by the choroid plexus and absorbed through the arachnoid granulations into the dural venous sinuses, especially the superior sagittal sinus.

cv-05c8ce40.stem: Where does the thoracic duct drain?
options: Into the left venous angle (junction of the left internal jugular and subclavian veins)
cv-05c8ce40.explanation: The thoracic duct, which collects most of the body's lymph, opens at the junction of the left internal jugular and subclavian veins; lymph from the right upper body reaches the right venous angle via the right lymphatic duct.

cv-9c435315.stem: In the fetal circulation, which vessel brings oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus?
cv-9c435315.explanation: The single umbilical vein brings oxygenated blood from the placenta; the two umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the placenta. Part of the blood bypasses the liver through the ductus venosus into the IVC.

cv-35606634.stem: Which nerve passes through the cavernous sinus itself (not in its wall)?
cv-35606634.explanation: The internal carotid artery and the abducens nerve pass through the sinus; III, IV, V1 and V2 run in its lateral wall. That is why the abducens is usually the first nerve affected in cavernous sinus thrombosis and ICA aneurysm.

cv-91f6535e.stem: A hypertensive patient has sudden, tearing chest pain radiating to the back and a marked blood pressure difference between the arms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
cv-91f6535e.explanation: In aortic dissection the inner layer tears and blood enters between the wall layers; because branch origins can be involved, pulse and blood pressure differ between the arms. Involvement of the ascending aorta (Stanford A) is a surgical emergency.

cv-5e60843b.stem: An elderly patient with atrial fibrillation has sudden abdominal pain out of proportion to the examination findings. What is the most likely cause?
cv-5e60843b.explanation: Because the SMA leaves the aorta at a narrow angle, emboli from the heart often lodge there; early acute mesenteric ischaemia gives very few examination findings compared with the severity of the pain.

cv-21fae810.stem: A patient who develops leg swelling and pain after a long flight is found to have deep vein thrombosis. What is the most serious complication?
cv-21fae810.explanation: A clot in the deep leg veins can break off and travel via the IVC and right heart into the pulmonary artery; massive pulmonary embolism can cause sudden death.

cv-ac08c79d.stem: Which of the following is NOT a component of tetralogy of Fallot?
cv-ac08c79d.explanation: Tetralogy of Fallot consists of VSD, pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta and right ventricular hypertrophy; it results from anterior displacement of the conal septum and is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease.

cv-5dd9592d.stem: What is the valve guarding the opening of the coronary sinus called?
options: Thebesian valve (valve of the coronary sinus)
cv-5dd9592d.explanation: The Thebesian valve lies where the coronary sinus opens into the right atrium, the Eustachian valve at the IVC opening. The tendon of Todaro is the continuation of the Eustachian valve and a border of Koch's triangle.

cv-9c344753.stem: Which vascular anomaly causes dysphagia lusoria (difficulty swallowing)?
options: A right subclavian artery arising as the last branch of the aortic arch and passing behind the oesophagus
cv-9c344753.explanation: The aberrant right subclavian artery (arteria lusoria) is the last branch of the aortic arch and crosses to the right behind the oesophagus, which it can compress; it is the most common aortic arch anomaly. The right recurrent laryngeal nerve is then non-recurrent.

cv-4fc98b11.stem: Which arteries are the most common source of hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage?
options: Cortical branches of the anterior cerebral artery
Lenticulostriate arteries (perforating branches of the middle cerebral artery)
cv-4fc98b11.explanation: The lenticulostriate arteries are thin end arteries arising at a right angle from the MCA; in chronic hypertension Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms develop and cause basal ganglia (putaminal) haemorrhages.

cv-79341972.stem: Which artery does NOT contribute to Kiesselbach's area, the source of most nosebleeds?
cv-79341972.explanation: Kiesselbach's (Little's) area on the anteroinferior septum is formed by anastomosing branches of the sphenopalatine, anterior ethmoidal, greater palatine and superior labial (facial) arteries.

cv-c5892b74.stem: What is the 'corona mortis', dangerous in hernia surgery?
options: The posterior trunk of the internal iliac artery
An anastomosis between the inferior epigastric (external iliac system) and obturator arteries crossing over the pubis
A connection between the right and left common iliac arteries
The deep branch of the femoral artery
An anastomosis between the superior and middle rectal arteries
cv-c5892b74.explanation: In some people the obturator artery (or vein) arises from, or widely anastomoses with, the external iliac/inferior epigastric system and crosses the superior pubic ramus. If injured in femoral hernia or pelvic surgery, severe bleeding occurs.

cv-edca0ec0.stem: What is the adult remnant of the ductus venosus?
cv-edca0ec0.explanation: In the fetus the ductus venosus carries blood from the umbilical vein past the liver into the IVC; after birth it closes to become the ligamentum venosum. The umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres hepatis.

cv-47659c1d.stem: What is the adult remnant of the umbilical vein?
options: Ligamentum teres hepatis (in the free edge of the falciform ligament)
cv-47659c1d.explanation: After birth the umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres hepatis. In portal hypertension the paraumbilical veins around this ligament open up and contribute to caput medusae.

cv-96f935f6.stem: What is the adult remnant of the distal part of the umbilical artery?
cv-96f935f6.explanation: The proximal part of the umbilical arteries stays patent as the superior vesical artery, the distal part becomes the medial umbilical ligament. The median umbilical ligament is the remnant of the urachus.

cv-d6da7df0.stem: What vessels are usually the source of a subdural haematoma?
options: Bridging veins running from the cortex to the dural sinuses
cv-d6da7df0.explanation: A subdural haematoma forms between dura and arachnoid when bridging veins, stretched by brain atrophy in the elderly and alcoholics, tear; it develops slowly and is crescent-shaped. An epidural haematoma usually arises from the middle meningeal artery.

cv-2151bfd7.stem: Which valveless venous network plays a role in the spread of prostate cancer to the spine?
cv-2151bfd7.explanation: Batson's plexus is a valveless venous network around the spine connected with the pelvic veins; when intra-abdominal pressure rises blood can flow towards the spine, explaining spinal spread of tumours such as prostate and breast cancer.

cv-88c74a4e.stem: In May–Thurner syndrome, which compression predisposes to deep vein thrombosis of the left leg?
options: Compression of the left femoral vein under the inguinal ligament
Compression of the inferior vena cava by the liver
Compression of the left common iliac vein against the spine by the right common iliac artery
Compression of the right external iliac vein by the sigmoid colon
Compression of the left renal vein between the aorta and SMA
cv-88c74a4e.explanation: The right common iliac artery crosses in front of the left common iliac vein and presses it against L5; over time a fibrous band forms in the vein wall and left leg DVT develops.

cv-ccd14bde.stem: A patient who squeezed a boil beside the nose develops fever, eyelid swelling, exophthalmos and double vision on lateral gaze. Which nerve is affected first, and why?
options: Facial nerve – because it runs with the facial vein
Optic nerve – because it lies in the wall of the sinus
Oculomotor nerve – because it passes through the sinus
Trochlear nerve – because it lies in the floor of the sinus
Abducens nerve – because it runs freely through the cavernous sinus
cv-ccd14bde.explanation: Infection in the danger triangle of the face spreads via the angular vein and superior ophthalmic vein to the cavernous sinus. The abducens nerve, running freely inside the sinus beside the ICA, is usually the first affected; lateral gaze is restricted.
